searchText: That's prolly not the case. The whole debate around eip-3756 and the gas limit began with miners voting for higher than 30mm The network is handling more gas than ever. Source: https://etherscan.io/chart/gasused And that's thanks to 1559, not in spite of it. The daily lows and highs you are quoting are from a much quieter time where did a miner vote higher than 30m? 30m could have been handled a year ago, it has nothing to do with 1559 it may have to do with clients that weren't optimized enough to do it then/now plenty of blocks like that 2 weeks ago: https://etherscan.io/blocks?ps=100&p=800 geth says it's a security issue: https://twitter.com/TimBeiko/status/1433837884457558048 the eip should just let devs set the limit, any perception of decentralization is gone if we're 100k gas from a DoS we may want those clients to do some work All of this is open source software. "we" can contribute if we can, and want to. "we" don't get to have demands. Client teams do listen and they know the software better than "we". If they discuss it, it means they know it's an issue The client devs are definitely working hard to mitigate every denial of service vector they find. This is a very hard problem on a censorship resistant platform, and there is rarely a simple solution. That being said, I actually consider the gas limit to be a censorship resistance issue. IMO, anyone should be able to run an Ethereum client on commodity hardware purchased for regular usage (not specialized for running Ethereum). You should be able to go to best buy, buy a laptop for day-to-day tasks and light gaming, get a normal internet connection for watching Netflix or whatever, and be able to run Ethereum in the background. That is very much not the case right now, and largely because of the state growth problem which is a function of the gas limit. With the transaction rates needed for the entire network it will not be possible for any 1 client to process all transactions in the fullness of time. It may be viable to run a shard if it's small enough. but to expect a raspberry pi to process 1/64th the network transactions may be over limiting We definitely want to scale Ethereum to support higher throughput. Layer 2 and sharding both help achieve this. There is also the research work on the Portal Network, State Expiry, and Regenesis to help mitigate the long term storage requirements of layer 1. None of those are available yet though, and I'm against the high operating requirements until they become available. Aside from Proof of Stake, pretty much all major research projects in Ethereum are related to scaling. There is a *lot* of effort being devoted to solving this problem, but it is a *really hard problem*. I don't know many laptops and desktops at best buy with 1tb of disk space, so I think that goal is lost for now. That could be pursued after regenesis Sharding would be a good time to drop the gas limits back to a much smaller size Yes, we very much are not hitting that target. The further we are from that target, the fewer end-users there are who are running an Ethereum client. IMO, we should not be making the situation worse than it already is, and high gas limits only amplify the problem, while low gas limits mitigate the problem. Guess that's a new opinion, gas limits have increased 2x this year. Not a new opinion, just not one shared by everyone (and not miners). I would think miners would want the smallest gas limit possible after 1559 as they could push the network into bidding wars after the blocks were full That is unlikely to occur. They are more likely to make money (short term) by having a higher gas limit because there are more transactions. The base fee will adjust up if the gas limit decreases, so miners won't get more. Good point, they actually want a volatile market. (nfts are perfect) Maybe instead of attacking me and saying Im a price cheerleader, you could do better to learn more first about how the EIP works and how to construct a better argument. Continuously saying EIP1559 is bad to the chain does not make it true, unless substantiated with proper data. https://discord.com/channels/595666850260713488/692078615269212180/881855787067125780 This is one of the data that you can use in your arguments, but even then this does not capture demand variability actually looking at that chart, the mean price seems to be the same. What disappeared is the low spikes In my experience that is the thing people are often frustrated with. They used to benefit from the market inefficiencies of pre-London which resulted in occasional really low dips. I *believe* this happened because the mempool cleared out after a medium length spike in demand, and then after the demand suddenly dropped gas prices went way down. My *suspicion* is that the block elasticity makes it so we no longer experience this same behavior of mempool clearing as people are better able to express their price preferences, so we no longer see the super low drops in gas price. I definitely understand this frustration, and the data backs it up However, that could all be bogus and in reality what we are seeing in those lows is just miners including things that don't make financial sense (like when they do their payouts with 1 nanoeth gas price). fair point, i didnt think of that On the other hand, I remember an analysis by Tim Roughgarden regarding benefits of the escalator algorithm with EIP1559. Is that something still to be considered in the future? <@!301186049323958275> do you know? I haven't heard of it discussed much. I personally don't think it is necessary, but I understand the theory behind why someone might want it. Right now you cannot really express time preference strongly without resorting to a traditional gas price auction. It would be nice if you could express something like "I want this to be included within the next five minutes, but I am otherwise not in a big hurry" vs "this needs to go in right now". as an outsider and a layman, looking at the paper review from Tim, I'm afraid it will introduce extra UX nightmare. But if it can be abstracted away from the user by wallet providers, it may be good $4.5 just sitting there because his wallet probably created a transaction with a high basefee but ended up paying less than that and got some money back but is now dust. Thats essentially also a fee burn. https://etherscan.io/address/0xe10509917a89c644095f807df2d27c8434b94dd0 would be interesting to see a chart of how much dust has been created after eip1559 due to it sending ETH back to an address that was being abandoned I would like to see someone propose an EIP that introduces a new transaction type for sweeping, where everything is transferred. would be nice if the user could specify whether the returned fee should go to the sending or receiving address linking to a simulation we did on 1559 + escalator. it shows pretty clearly that once again the 1559 component of fees adjusting to price out most of the demand eventually dominate, so should the escalator be useful, it would really only be in these times of demand changes, and even then it might be hard to parameterise properly: https://ethereum.github.io/abm1559/notebooks/floatingEscalator.html not claiming this settles the question, the simulation was more exploratory in nature, but I don't personally see it being implemented in protocol anytime soon
